## Overview

The Census Bureau's Population Estimates Program (PEP) produces annual
population and housing unit estimates for the nation, states, and
counties between decennial census years. Rather than conducting a new
count each year, PEP applies a demographic balancing equation: each
year's population estimate starts from the prior year's count, adds
births, subtracts deaths, and adds net migration (both domestic and
international). Housing unit estimates are built separately from the
decennial census baseline, incorporating permitted construction,
non-permitted construction, mobile home shipments, and estimated housing
loss. The result is a consistent annual series that captures how and
why population and housing stock are changing — not just whether they
are.

The components-of-change approach is what makes PEP analytically
valuable beyond the headline total. Two counties can have identical
population growth rates driven by entirely different dynamics: one
growing through natural increase, another through working-age
in-migration, a third through retiree in-migration. PEP makes those
distinctions visible at the county level every year, which the
decennial census alone cannot provide.

## What This Data Tells Us About Rural America

Population estimates are a foundational input to rural economic
analysis, but their value lies in the components of change rather than
the headline net figure. A community growing at 0.5% per year through
natural increase and retiree in-migration is building a very different
demographic and economic future than one growing at the same rate through
working-age in-migration. The Population Estimates Program provides the
annual county-level components — births, deaths, domestic net migration,
international net migration — that make this disaggregation possible.

For rural communities, population trends reflect the cumulative effect
of economic conditions, quality of life, and community capacity over
time. Out-migration of working-age residents is a persistent pattern in
many rural counties. CORI's research suggests this is not always
reversed by improvements in economic indicators alone — factors beyond
employment and income appear to shape migration decisions. PEP reveals
what demographic flows are occurring; understanding why requires pairing
it with other data and community context. Understanding which flows are
driving population change is the starting point for identifying which
conditions matter most.

PEP tells us not just whether a rural community is growing or shrinking,
but what is driving that change: births and deaths, domestic migration,
and international migration. Those distinctions matter because different
population trajectories imply different workforce, housing, service, and
economic-development challenges.

## Coverage

- **Geography:** County, State, National
- **Time range:** 2000–present (CORI package); PEP data available
  further back at state and national levels from the Census Bureau
  directly
- **Update frequency:** Annual; released each spring for the prior
  calendar year
- **Universe:** Resident civilian population of the United States;
  estimates are anchored to decennial census benchmarks and revised
  with each new vintage

::: callout-note
**Vintage revisions:** PEP revises the full time series within each
intercensal decade with each annual release. Estimates from 2020–present
may differ from earlier releases as new data refines the components.
When a new decennial census is conducted, the entire prior decade's
estimates are reconciled to the new benchmark. Analysts should use a
consistent vintage when comparing population or components of change
across years. See the [PEP methodology
page](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/popest/technical-documentation/methodology.html)
for documentation of component data sources and estimation procedures.
:::

## Key Variables

**Population totals** (`get_population()`)

- `population` — total resident population estimate
- `population_16plus` — population age 16 and over (used as labor force
  denominator in employment rate calculations)

**Components of change** (`get_population_change()`)

- `births` — live births
- `deaths` — deaths
- `natural_change` — births minus deaths
- `domestic_migration` — net domestic in-migration (people moving from
  other U.S. counties)
- `international_migration` — net international in-migration
- `net_migration` — domestic plus international net migration

## Accessing the Data

### Via CORI R Package

The [`cori.data.pep`](/packages/cori-data-pep/) package provides tidy
access to PEP population totals and components of change at the county,
state, and national level from 2000 to the present. Because PEP produces consistent annual county populations, it is also a
highly convenient resource for converting raw counts into per-capita
rates — a best practice for comparing counties of very different sizes
that makes rural and nonrural comparisons genuinely apples-to-apples.

```r
library(cori.data.pep)

# Total population — all counties, all years
get_population(geography = "county", variables = "population")

# Components of change — specific counties
get_population_change(
  variables = c("domestic_migration", "international_migration",
                "natural_change"),
  geoids = grep("^54", unique(get_population(geography = "county")$geoid),
                value = TRUE),
  years = 2010:2025
)
```

### Direct from Source

Annual estimate files are available for download from the [Census
Population and Housing Unit Estimates
page](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/popest.html). Files are
organized by vintage year and geography. See the [PEP methodology
page](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/popest/technical-documentation/methodology.html)
for full documentation of component data sources, estimation methods,
and vintage revision procedures.
